name: Emeka Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Emeka. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the acute medical unit, which is where people land after A&E before they go to a proper ward. It's fast: someone arrives with sepsis, someone else with a bleed, and you're doing obs, cannulas, fluids and calling the doctor every twenty minutes. I like the pace and the puzzles. What wears me out is that I'm still the junior who gets told to slow down and check his drug calculations twice.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned checking calculations. How do you handle the bits you're still learning?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, I use AI a lot outside work. I quiz myself with a chatbot on the bus about drug interactions, and I built a little flashcard deck for sepsis protocols. At work I stick to the hospital's systems, but I'm always the one asking IT when the new features come. My sister calls me the ward's unpaid tech guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I'd be a little disappointed, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, because the NHS could really use smart tools that cut paperwork. I'd probably post something about how the tech was oversold and the money should have gone into staffing instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job's safe either way. Acute medicine needs hands and judgement, and there aren't enough of us. I'd still be paying my rent, sending a hundred a month to my mum in Leeds, and saving what I can, which is about three months' worth now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. I'd finish my preceptorship, that's the first-year support programme for new nurses, and then apply for the acute care course. I'd keep using AI for my own study because it helps me. I quiz myself on drug interactions with a chatbot on the bus, and in this picture the hospital would never catch up with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe. I like change, and this picture has very little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your plans if nothing much changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably aim for a senior post on the unit in four or five years. Maybe try for a nurse informatics role, which is the people who design the hospital's computer systems, but that's a bonus, not the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about money that bothers you even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent going up and my mum's heating bills. Sending her money means I don't save as fast as my friends. But I've got a steady job, so it doesn't keep me up.

say: It's a **shame**, because the NHS needs tools that cut paperwork.
The money should have gone into **staffing** instead of hype.
think: My job is **safe either way**, because acute medicine needs hands.
Sending **£100 a month** to my mum slows my savings, but it's steady.
do: Apply for the **acute care course** afterwards.
Keep using AI for **my own study** on the bus.
feel: **Calm** and a little flat, because he likes change.
S0.quote: I quiz myself on drug interactions with a chatbot on the bus, and in this picture the hospital would never catch up with that.
fieldNote: An **early adopter** who's disappointed rather than relieved by a plateau.
His job security is **solid**, with pressure coming from family support.
He already has a quiet interest in **nurse informatics**.

steps.text: Finish the first-year preceptorship on the acute medical unit
Keep using a chatbot to quiz himself on drug interactions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one I'd actually want, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for nurses if we're in the room when it's designed. AI doing the bed booking, the discharge letters and checking drug doses is great, but only if nurses help build it. I'd be posting about nurse-led design.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. The hands-on bit of my job stays, and the paperwork shrinks. Being the nurse who already uses AI every day stops being a joke and starts being a career. I might move up faster than I would otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to be a super-user, that's the person on the ward who learns the new system first and helps everyone else. I'd ask about the nurse informatics training. I'd push the union to have nurses on the committee that picks the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit guilty for the ward clerks, but excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ward clerk, Joy, who's about sixty. She books every bed and chases every result. I'd want her retrained, not dropped. I'd say that to managers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move up faster. Isn't that a bit selfish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit. But if I'm the one helping colleagues use the system, I'm helping patients too. And I'd still be the junior on obs and cannulas for a while yet.

say: This is good for nurses only if we're **in the room** when it's built.
think: Paperwork shrinks while the **hands-on bit** stays, which suits me.
Being an **everyday AI user** could help me move up faster.
do: Volunteer as the ward's **super-user** for the new system.
Push the union for nurses on the **tool selection** committee.
feel: **Excited**, with some guilt for the ward clerks.
S1.quote: Being the nurse who already uses AI every day stops being a joke and starts being a career.
fieldNote: He sees this world as a **career opening**, not a threat.
He still names the **ward clerk** as someone who'd suffer.
His progressive views show in wanting **nurse-led** tool design.

steps.text: Volunteer as the acute unit's super-user for new AI tools
Ask the practice educator about nurse informatics training
Push the union to put nurses on the tool selection committee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. Okay, that's different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be shared. If machines can do the thinking work, the wealth has to go to people, through things like a basic income and public ownership of the big systems. I'd be campaigning for that, loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the thinking parts of my job would be gone by 2028: calculating doses, spotting sepsis early, planning the shift. I'd be fine with that for a few years because I still do the hands-on work. But robots by 2031 is when I'd really worry, because a junior nurse with a two-year diploma isn't hard to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on learning how these systems work in a hospital, so I'm the human who checks the AI and the robots. I'd save harder, maybe four hundred a month instead of two hundred, and cut my nights out. I'd also join every campaign for public control of this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Part of me is thrilled at the science, and part of me thinks about my mum's heating money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm fine for now and I'm learning the new stuff. I wouldn't tell her about the robot bit, she'd just worry and start sending money back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're excited but anxious. Which wins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, on a bad night. Excited, on a good day. The difference is whether I'm the one supervising the robots or the one they replaced.

say: The wealth has to be **shared**, through basic income and public ownership.
I'd **campaign loudly** for public control of these systems.
think: The **thinking parts** of my job are gone by 2028.
Robots by **2031** make a junior with a diploma easy to replace.
do: Learn how hospital **AI and robots** work, to become the human checker.
Double savings to about **£400 a month**.
Join campaigns for **public control** of AI.
feel: **Anxious** on bad nights, thrilled by the science on good days.
S2.quote: Robots by 2031 is when I'd really worry, because a junior nurse with a two-year diploma isn't hard to replace.
fieldNote: Even the most adaptive nurse becomes **anxious** at a five-year robot deadline.
He hides the **robot risk** from his mum to protect her.
His plan is to become the **human checker**, a role he isn't sure exists.

steps.text: Learn how ward AI and robots work to become their checker
Cut nights out and save about £400 a month
Join campaigns for public ownership of AI systems

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more like a proper career plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing as before, that the gains must be shared, but I'd say it with more hope because there's time to set it up properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is perfect for me to get into nurse informatics. By 2031 I'd have the experience and maybe the master's to be one of the people deciding how AI is used on wards. Robots around 2034 still worry me, but I'd be on the right side of the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my preceptorship, then apply for an informatics secondment in 2028. I'd save a bit more, maybe three hundred a month. And I'd keep using AI every day in my own study so I really understand its limits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a hopeful way. It's still fast, but I can see a path through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That everyone has the same idea. If every tech-minded nurse goes for informatics, there won't be enough jobs, so I'd need to be good, not just keen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to fund a master's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My car, probably, and the holiday I was planning to Lagos with my cousins. That one would hurt.

say: The gains must be **shared**, and five years is time to set that up.
I'd say it with more **hope** this time.
think: Five years is enough to get into **nurse informatics**.
By **2031** I could be deciding how AI is used on wards.
do: Save about **£300 a month** for a possible master's.
Keep using AI daily to learn its **limits**.
feel: **Uneasy** but hopeful, seeing a path through.
S3.quote: If every tech-minded nurse goes for informatics, there won't be enough jobs, so I'd need to be good, not just keen.
fieldNote: He sees five years as a **perfect window** for his career switch.
He's honest about **competition** for informatics jobs.
Giving up the **Lagos trip** is his painful trade-off.

steps.text: Apply for a nurse informatics secondment in 2028
Sell the car and save about £300 a month for a master's
Keep testing AI tools daily to learn where they fail

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's basically my whole early career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to get this right. Nurses should be designing these systems, and governments should be planning how to share the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is plenty. I'd have the master's, experience on the acute unit, and probably an informatics role by the time AGI comes in 2036. Robots around 2039 would be something I help bring in, not something that happens to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much what I'd do anyway, just steadier. Preceptorship, acute care course, then the informatics master's around 2029. Save steadily. Keep pushing the union to think about this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Ten years feels like a career, not a countdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything worry you even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum. She's on her own and her pension is small. If the economy changes a lot, she's the one I'd worry about, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still send her money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Always. Maybe more, once I'm earning more. That's non-negotiable.

say: We've got **time** to get this right, so let's not waste it.
Nurses should be **designing** these systems, and governments planning how to share the gains.
think: Ten years means I'd have a **master's** and an informatics role by 2036.
Robots around **2039** would be something I help bring in.
do: Finish the **acute care course** after preceptorship.
Keep sending money to **my mum**, maybe more.
feel: **Calm**, because ten years feels like a career, not a countdown.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like a career, not a countdown.
fieldNote: With a decade, he sees himself **leading** the change rather than reacting to it.
His worry shifts entirely to his **mum's small pension**.
Family support stays **non-negotiable** in every picture he describes.

steps.text: Start a nurse informatics master's around 2029
Complete the acute care course on the medical unit
Keep sending his mum in Leeds money every month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots would come before I've built up any experience. What would help is a proper public plan for sharing the gains, and hospitals training nurses to run and check these systems rather than just replacing us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about older nurses. I'm young and I like this stuff. Joy and the senior nurses who've done thirty years by hand need real support, not a two-hour e-learning module. Ten years makes me calm, but they'd need more than time.

headlineQuote: Joy and the senior nurses who've done thirty years by hand need real support, not a two-hour e-learning module.
portrait: Emeka is a **27-year-old junior nurse** on an acute medical unit who uses AI daily for his own study.
He sends **£100 a month** to his mum and has about three months saved.
He's **progressive**, wanting nurses to design tools and the gains shared publicly.
He stays **calm** in slow pictures but turns anxious when robots arrive by 2031.
His plan across every picture is a path into **nurse informatics**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots would arrive before he'd built real experience.
whatWouldHelp: A **public plan** to share the gains from AI.
Hospitals **training nurses** to run and check AI rather than replacing them.
